title: A qualified name is absolute, and the leading `\` does not parse
scope:
how a name written in source — a class, interface, enum, `type` alias or attribute
reference — resolves to a fully-qualified name, and the spelling of the `namespace` declaration
itself. Not in scope: *what* may be imported and under which short name
([0015](0015.md)), the `Core` prefix's reservation
([0011](0011.md) § 2), how a name's case is compared
([0062](0062.md) § 1), or which file a name is loaded from
([0061](0061.md)).
dependsOnText:
[0011](0011.md) — removing free functions
and constants is what leaves classes as the only kind of name to resolve, and so what makes PHP's
fallback-to-global rule removable rather than load-bearing.

summary.headline: A name containing a backslash is always read from the root
summary.body:
`App\Models\User` means the same thing in every file, wherever it is written. A name with no
backslash is short, and is resolved through the file's imports and then its own namespace,
nowhere else. There is no relative form — inside `namespace App;`, writing `Models\User` does
not find `App\Models\User` — and importing `Core\Json` does not let you write `Json\Derive`; an
import binds one whole name, never a prefix. A leading backslash does not parse at all, and the
error names the spelling without it. One rule decides every name.
